query: Why do expense decline rates differ across departments?

per_column.name: department_decline_rate
per_column.rationale: This is the per-department decline rate itself -- the focus outcome whose variation across departments is being explained. It restates the target, not a cause.

per_column.name: department_avg_amount
per_column.rationale: Average expense amount per department could plausibly influence both scrutiny/approval behaviour (a candidate treatment) and the decline rate (higher-value expenses more likely questioned). Not named in the query, so it is a surfaced common-cause candidate. However, no explicit treatment exists for it to confound, weakening its role.

per_column.name: is_declined
per_column.rationale: Row-level declined indicator is the raw form of the outcome (decline event), not a treatment or confounder.

judge.rationale: The added columns fail the causal-attribution test. Two of the three (department_decline_rate, is_declined) are simply the outcome restated at department and row level -- they add no cause. No TREATMENT (candidate cause whose effect on decline rate is being attributed) is supplied at all, so requirement (a) is unmet. Only department_avg_amount is a plausible non-query variable, but with no treatment present it has nothing to confound, and it is at best a weak common-cause candidate rather than part of an articulated identification strategy. There is no set-up for causal estimation: no treatment/confounder pairing that would let the department differences be attributed to an adjusted cause.
